First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}+4 & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =-1 \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=-1$ is our only real solution. Since $-1\in [-2,1]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=-1.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14030836/assets/b0f2899bf6a946f6d7bf8bc60c41827bd05aef500f0fc0f30a5916c26b1007bb.png)

Notice that the region for $x\in [-2,-1]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{-1}(4{x}^{3}+4)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{-2}^{-1}(4{x}^{3}+4)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4{\int }_{-2}^{-1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x-4{\int }_{-2}^{-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{x}^{4}{|}_{-2}^{-1}-4x{|}_{-2}^{-1} \\  & =-[(-1)^{4}-(-2)^{4}]-4[-1+2] \\  & =-(-15)-4 \\  & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [-1,1]$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(4{x}^{3}+4)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+4{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{4}{|}_{-1}^{1}+4x{|}_{-1}^{-1} \\  & =[{1}^{4}-(-1)^{4}]+4[1-(-1)] \\  & =0+8 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=11+8=19.
$$

authoring.value:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x(3-x) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $3\in [1,4],$ we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=3.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=3$ to $x=4.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013598/assets/219d7aa5b976c97d47a96d0c94c3d61d139d5ddddc55b82d0df68f19ad6d5149.png)

Notice that the region for $x\in [3,4]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{3}^{4}(3x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(3x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{3}x\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{1}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}\,{|}_{1}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}\,{|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[{3}^{2}-{1}^{2}]-\frac{1}{3}[{3}^{3}-{1}^{3}] \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[9-1]-\frac{1}{3}[27-1] \\  & =12-\frac{26}{3} \\  & =\frac{10}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [3,4],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =-{\int }_{3}^{4}(3x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3{\int }_{3}^{4}x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{4}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}\,{|}_{3}^{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}\,{|}_{3}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}[{4}^{2}-{3}^{2}]+\frac{1}{3}[{4}^{3}-{3}^{3}] \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}[16-9]+\frac{1}{3}[64-27] \\  & =-\frac{21}{2}+\frac{37}{3} \\  & =\frac{11}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=\frac{10}{3}+\frac{11}{6}=\frac{31}{6}.
$$

authoring.value:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}27-3{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2} & =27 \\ {x}^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=-3$ and $x=3$ are our real solutions. Since $3\in [-3,5]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=3.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=3$ to $x=5.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013598/assets/6b3ca7be487585b296aaeb0b3fa7eb4ce8b9b4f9ad35d52baefa04f2fbbed621.png)

For $x\in [-3,3]$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{3}(27-3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =27{\int }_{-3}^{3}\,\text{d}x-3{\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =27x{|}_{-3}^{3}-{x}^{3}{|}_{-3}^{3} \\  & =27[3-(-3)]-[(3)^{3}-(-3)^{3}] \\  & =162-54 \\  & =108.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that for $x\in [3,5]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{3}^{5}(27-3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =-{\int }_{3}^{5}(27-3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-27{\int }_{3}^{5}\,\text{d}x+3{\int }_{3}^{5}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-27x{|}_{3}^{5}+{x}^{3}{|}_{3}^{5} \\  & =-27[5-3]+[(5)^{3}-(3)^{3}] \\  & =-54+98 \\  & =44.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=108+44=152.
$$

authoring.value:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-9x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-9) & =0 \\ x(x-3)(x+3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=0,$ $x=-3,$ and $x=3$ are our real solutions. Since $0 \in [-3,3]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013598/assets/29a51c9892de59037e84bace2f8b5822222c3056a05af861cbd741390a437a61.png)

For $x \in [-3,0]$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{0}({x}^{3}-9x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{0}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x-9{\int }_{-3}^{0}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}{|}_{-3}^{0}-\frac{9{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{-3}^{0} \\  & =[0-\frac{(-3)^{4}}{4}]-9[0-\frac{(-3)^{2}}{2}] \\  & =-\frac{81}{4}+\frac{81}{2} \\  & =\frac{81}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that for $x \in [0,3]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
\int_{a}^{b} y(x) \:\textrm{d}x = \int_{0}^{3} \left(x^3-9x\right) \:\textrm{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{3}-9x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+9{\int }_{0}^{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}{|}_{0}^{3}+\frac{9{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-[\frac{(3)^{4}}{4}-0]+9[\frac{(3)^{2}}{2}-0] \\  & =-\frac{81}{4}+\frac{81}{2} \\  & =\frac{81}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A = A_1+A_2 =  \dfrac{81}{4} + \dfrac{81}{4} = \dfrac{81}{2}.
$$
